Stage 01

Pre-Incorporation & Know-Your-Customer

UBO transparency, Apostille authentication chain, official name clearance restricted wordlist, and pre-incorporation statutory fee budget.

UBO Ultimate Beneficial Owner Screening Rules Official Registry Only

>=25% ownership / control

Applicable AML statute: Ley 10/2010, de 28 de abril, de prevención del blanqueo de capitales y de la financiación del terrorismo, as amended; Real Decreto 304/2014, de 5 de mayo, Reglamento de la Ley 10/2010; Real Decreto 1784/1996, de 19 de julio, Reglamento del Registro Mercantil; Directive (EU) 2015/849 and Directive (EU) 2018/843 (AMLD5) as transposed; Registro de Titularidades Reales — created under art. 4.2 of Ley 10/2010 and developed by Real Decreto 304/2014 (arts. 7-21), subject to the operational criteria of the Registradores de España.
Registered Agent & Physical Address Licensed Agent Required

A virtual office address is conditionally accepted for provisional commercial registration by the Mercantile Registry, but it cannot consist merely of a P.O. Box. For a Sociedad de Responsabilidad Limitada dedicated to trade supply-chain factoring and reverse factoring, SEPBLAC and the applicable AML/CFT framework require a physical office in Spain where the compliance officer (Representante ante el SEPBLAC), records, personnel, and operational systems are accessible. A virtual-only address creates a high risk of denial of the factoring-related license application, adverse commercial substance findings, tax residence challenges, and enhanced inspection.

✓ Partner licensed company-secretary channels provide local registered address and government mail forwarding.

Stage 02

Statutory Formation & Board Resolutions

Competent registry, governing statute, capital lockup rules, and first board resolution template.

Competent corporate registry

The relevant provincial Mercantile Registry (Registro Mercantil Provincial), with name-certification functions performed by the Central Mercantile Registry (Registro Mercantil Central).

Governing statute

Royal Legislative Decree 1/2010 approving the Spanish Companies Act (Ley de Sociedades de Capital), particularly Articles 4, 19-30, 58-62, 78-83, 210-242, and 249-252; Royal Decree 1784/1996 approving the Mercantile Registry Regulations; Law 14/2013 and applicable electronic incorporation procedures.

Formation / constitutional filings

Notarial public deed of incorporation (escritura pública de constitución), together with the application for registration in the provincial Mercantile Registry and the company bylaws.

Incorporation processing time

⚡ 273 business days (SOP sum)

Paid-up Capital & Blocked Account Regime No Capital Lockup Account Required

A standard Sociedad de Responsabilidad Limitada may be incorporated with minimum capital of EUR 1. Capital must be fully subscribed and paid at incorporation. If capital is below EUR 3,000, statutory reserve and shareholder-liability safeguards apply until the company reaches EUR 3,000. A company professionally conducting factoring as a regulated financial-credit activity must obtain authorization as an Establecimiento Financiero de Crédito and generally maintain minimum share capital of EUR 5 million, fully paid in cash or qualifying assets, subject to the applicable prudential framework. Spain has no single fixed state incorporation filing fee denominated in USD; notarial, registry, name-certification, tax, translation, legalization, and professional charges are separate.

Funding & unlock path: Obtain the applicable municipal fire-safety and opening clearance, maintain emergency exits, evacuation procedures, fire equipment, accessibility measures, and occupancy compliance, and obtain structural or load certification where construction or heavy equipment is introduced. Comply with Law 31/1995 on Occupational Risk Prevention, prepare risk assessments and emergency procedures, and document employee training and preventive services. No factory-specific industrial safety clearance is normally required for a conventional office.

Paid-in capital rule: A standard Sociedad de Responsabilidad Limitada may be incorporated with minimum capital of EUR 1. Capital must be fully subscribed and paid at incorporation. If capital is below EUR 3,000, statutory reserve and shareholder-liability safeguards apply until the company reaches EUR 3,000. A company professionally conducting factoring as a regulated financial-credit activity must obtain authorization as an Establecimiento Financiero de Crédito and generally maintain minimum share capital of EUR 5 million, fully paid in cash or qualifying assets, subject to the applicable prudential framework. Spain has no single fixed state incorporation filing fee denominated in USD; notarial, registry, name-certification, tax, translation, legalization, and professional charges are separate.

Industrial Access / EIA & Civil Defense Approval Mandatory Environmental Clearance

For regulated factoring, the Bank of Spain and the Ministry of Economy, Trade and Enterprise under the Establecimientos Financieros de Crédito framework. For premises, the relevant municipal Ayuntamiento and, where applicable, the competent autonomous-community industrial authority.

Category: Authorization to operate as an Establecimiento Financiero de Crédito, including professional lending and factoring activities; separately, a municipal activity, opening, or responsible-declaration filing may be required for the physical office.

Stage 03

Tax Identity & Indirect Tax

Tax authority e-portal, entity tax classification elections, VAT thresholds, and 0% export documentation chain.

Tax ID Application Infrastructure

Competent tax authority

Agencia Estatal de Administración Tributaria (AEAT) - Sede Electrónica (sede.agenciatributaria.gob.es)

E-government filing portal

A Spanish Sociedad de Responsabilidad Limitada (SL) obtains its definitive NIF (Número de Identificación Fiscal) from AEAT after notarial incorporation and registration in the Registro Mercantil, using form 036/037 and identifying a legal administrator. Non-resident foreign entities without a permanent establishment that undertake taxable operations in Spain must obtain a non-resident NIF through AEAT (form 036), file an application signed by a tax representative in Spain, and submit apostilled or legalized corporate registration documents, articles of incorporation, certificate of foreign tax residence, and a sworn Spanish translation of all relevant instruments. The AEAT will issue a definitive NIF once the officer verifies identity and Spanish fiscal address details.

Tax ID type & application path: Entity_Level_Taxation — A Spanish Sociedad de Responsabilidad Limitada (SL) obtains its definitive NIF (Número de Identificación Fiscal) from AEAT after notarial incorporation and registration in the Registro Mercantil, using form 036/037 and identifying a legal administrator. Non-resident foreign entities without a permanent establishment that undertake taxable operations in Spain must obtain a non-resident NIF through AEAT (form 036), file an application signed by a tax representative in Spain, and submit apostilled or legalized corporate registration documents, articles of incorporation, certificate of foreign tax residence, and a sworn Spanish translation of all relevant instruments. The AEAT will issue a definitive NIF once the officer verifies identity and Spanish fiscal address details.

Default Tax Classification & Elections

Default tax classification

Entity_Level_Taxation

Available election forms

Spain does not operate a check-the-box regime. Spanish resident SLs are automatically treated as separate taxable entities subject to Impuesto sobre Sociedades. Available elections include the consolidated corporate tax filing regime for 90%+ controlled groups, special transparency regimes for temporary joint ventures (UTE) and economic interest groupings (AIE), the reduced start-up corporation rate, IP Box partial exemption, and R&D tax credit special allocation. Hybrid mismatch rules under ATAD are mandatory and not elective; Spain has no elective hybrid anti-avoidance mechanism.

VAT / GST & 0% Export Zero-Rating

Standard VAT / GST rate

21%

Mandatory registration threshold (Nexus)

No general VAT registration de minimis threshold; a taxable person must register with AEAT before first taxable supply. For intra-EU distance sales, the optional One-Stop-Shop simplification threshold is EUR 10,000; exceeding that threshold requires Spanish VAT registration or OSS reporting in the Member State of establishment.

Real-time VAT information reporting applies under the Suministro Inmediato de Información (SII) system for large taxpayers with turnover over EUR 6,000,000, VAT groups, and entities in the red/blue registration lists. The upcoming Veri*Factu regime (implementing Law 28/2022 and Crea y Crece) mandates B2B electronic invoicing with certified invoicing software, QR-linked digital verification code, and machine-readable invoice files submitted to AEAT through interoperable APIs. Exports and intra-community supplies must be reflected in customs declarations or periodic EU recapitulative statements.

Stage 04

Banking & Treasury Architecture

Central-bank FX diagnosis, tier-1 local banks vs offshore digital EMI matrix, and KYC rejection defense guide.

Foreign Exchange Regime & Central Bank Policy

Current-account convertibility

Spain applies the eurozone's full liberalisation: the euro is freely convertible on both current and capital account, and no exchange-control licensing, surrender requirements, or approval is required for commercial or financial transfers (Law 19/2003, of 4 July, on the legal regime of capital movements and external economic transactions; Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union arts. 63–66; OECD Codes of Liberalisation). Profit remittance from a Spanish SL is unrestricted, subject only to: (i) corporate income tax compliance and the documentary burden for treaty-based dividend withholding relief (default 19% non-resident withholding; reduced rate available on submission of Form 210, tax-residence certificate, and UBO certification); and (ii) statistical declarations to Banco de España. The effective hurdles for a factoring entity are banking KYC/AML for the originator and the practical need to evidence beneficial ownership in the SL according to Law 10/2010.

Export proceeds surrender rules

There is no statutory surrender or mandatory conversion of export proceeds in Spain. Spanish exporters and their assignees (including a factoring company holding assigned export receivables) may maintain receipts in EUR or foreign currency, effect investment abroad, and repatriate funds without prior approval. Transactions of EUR 50,000 or more per operation are reportable to Banco de España for balance-of-payments and monetary statistics, using the Bank's operation-classifier codes; for direct-investment movements of EUR 3,005,060.52 or more, DGCIIN registration is obligatory, and non-EU FDI in sensitive sectors (e.g., defence, dual-use, critical infrastructure, media) remains subject to the RDL 34/2020 prior-authorisation regime.

Central bank supervision: Banco de España (Bank of Spain), acting as the Eurosystem National Central Bank, together with the Dirección General de Comercio Internacional e Inversiones (DGCIIN) of the Ministry of Economy, Trade and Business for foreign-investment recording and FDI screening; the Comisión de Prevención del Blanqueo de Capitales e Infracciones Monetarias (SEPBLAC) supervises AML/CTF countermeasures for the regulated sector.

Offshore Digital Bank / EMI Whitelist

Cross-border EMI / Fintech rails Fit: High

Rating: LOW as the primary/sole liquidity host; MEDIUM as an ancillary collections or multi-currency wallet layer. Pursuant to Spanish Law 21/2011 on electronic money and the PSD2-derived regime (Royal Decree-Law 19/2017, Royal Decree 130/2019), only an electronic-money institution (EMI) or payment institution authorised or passported in the EEA may lawfully provide e-money, payment accounts, and payment services in Spain. An offshore digital EMI (post-Brexit UK EMI, US or LatAm fintech) that lacks EEA passporting rights has no regulated access to the Spanish market: it cannot open Spanish IBAN accounts, settle Spanish staff costs, or receive Spanish debtor collections with the same legal comfort as a credit institution. Such offshore EMIs may be used purely as a technical add-in via a contractual agency model with an EEA-authorised EMI/bank; they cannot confer the creditor-protection, factoring-escrow, or LC-issuance capabilities needed for a licensed trade-finance company.

Core KYC Rejection Triggers & Defense Dossier

Opaque UBO chain or nominee shareholding concealing the natural-person beneficiary of the factoring company.

Root cause: Opaque UBO chain or nominee shareholding concealing the natural-person beneficiary of the factoring company.

Defense evidence: Notarised certificate of the Libro Registro de Socios; updated Mercantile Registry (Registro Mercantil) transcript; UBO self-declaration identifying all natural persons holding more than 25%; notarised powers of attorney; apostilled passport copies of shareholders and directors; Spanish tax-residence certificates; and audited financial statements evidencing the source of paid-in capital.
Duplicate or concurrent assignment of the same trade receivables ('double factoring' or non-verified reverse-factoring) creating layering risk.

Root cause: Duplicate or concurrent assignment of the same trade receivables ('double factoring' or non-verified reverse-factoring) creating layering risk.

Defense evidence: Chronologically stamped receivables assignment register; debtor notification letters with acknowledgement receipts; registration with the Spanish factoring registry/association to evidence first-in-time assignment; certified invoice ledger tied to VAT/SII records; audit-confirmation circularisation to debtor accounts-payable departments; and legal opinions confirming absence of non-assignment clauses in the underlying supply contracts.
Sanctioned or high-risk counterparties appearing in the invoice chain or settlement instructions.

Root cause: Sanctioned or high-risk counterparties appearing in the invoice chain or settlement instructions.

Defense evidence: Automated screening report covering EU consolidated financial-sanctions lists and OFAC SDN; passport/business-register extraction for each debtor and supplier; SWIFT MT199 bank-reference letters; jurisdiction-risk memorandum; full-chain trade documents (purchase orders, bills of lading, CMR waybills, customs declarations) proving the genuine movement of goods; and a contractual undertaking to cease funding upon any sanctions designation.
Third-party or split payments not matching the assigned invoice (indirect payment red flag).

Root cause: Third-party or split payments not matching the assigned invoice (indirect payment red flag).

Defense evidence: Written payment-direction letter from the debtor; assignment-notice clause in the factoring agreement; transactional matching output from the treasury workstation; proof-of-delivery, freight and customs documentation; debtor-side confirmation of accepted goods/services; and a dual-authorisation manual override protocol for any departure from the matched schedule.
Invoice-financing for shell trading vehicles lacking operational substance and historic cash-flow track record.

Root cause: Invoice-financing for shell trading vehicles lacking operational substance and historic cash-flow track record.

Defense evidence: Rental contract for registered office and warehouse; Spanish social-security and payroll records evidencing staff substance; audited financial statements for at least three years; AEAT tax-compliance and SII/VAT filing certificates; warehouse receipts, insurance certificates and inspection reports; and independent auditor or board-minute evidence of physical trade flows.

Cross-Border Clearing Corridors & Settlement Fit

Equity injections into the Spanish SL should be routed as SWIFT MT103/ISO 20022 pacs.008 credits from the shareholder's bank to the SL's capital escrow account, with Remittance Information (field 70) stating the purpose—e.g., 'Aporte de capital social / liberación de capital' or 'Préstamo mercantil intragrupo'—and the beneficiary bank's classification code under Banco de España's balance-of-payments classifier. The incoming credit must be pre-flagged to the receiving bank to avoid statistical misclassification as trade payment. For inbound FDI, the DGCIIN declaration is required where the investment equals or exceeds EUR 3,005,060.52; non-EU residents investing in sensitive sectors (critical infrastructure, critical technology, media, defence/dual-use, or acquiring a 10%+ stake in a strategic listed company) are subject to prior-authorisation monitoring under RDL 34/2020. Supporting documents for bank release: shareholders' capital-increase deed (notarised and registered), registry certificate, a capital confirmation letter, and the agreed FDI declaration where applicable.For EU-disbursements (supplier payments under reverse factoring), use SEPA Credit Transfers (SCT, XML ISO 20022 pacs.008) settled in T2 real-time gross settlement; for non-EU/suppliers in foreign currency, use SWIFT MT103 wires with the unique end-to-end transaction reference (UETR) and appropriate Banco de España statistical purpose codes. For documentary trade, utilise SWIFT MT700/MT710 confirmed commercial letters of credit under UCP 600, or MT759/MT760 standby letters of credit and demand guarantees subject to URDG 758. Factoring and confirming receipts are settled by the factor to the supplier upon verified invoice and delivery data; the factor's bank should provide a segregated disbursement sub-ledger and a 'confirming' module to match assigned invoices, thereby preserving audit trail and preventing commingling of client money.Deliverable FX forwards (EUR/USD and EUR/LatAm crosses), executed under an ISDA/CSA or bank credit-line framework, with daily margin and settlement via CLS or correspondent clearing.Non-deliverable forwards (NDFs) for restricted-currency exposures arising from debtor payments in Latin American and EMEA non-convertible currencies, cash-settled in EUR or USD.Cross-currency interest-rate swaps (CCIRS) to swap foreign-currency floating-rate factoring funding (e.g., USD asset-backed lines) into EUR, aligning funding and receivable currencies.Vanilla FX options (EUR call/put combinations) to hedge downside on illiquid debtor portfolios while retaining upside; options may also be embedded in confirmed reverse-factoring structures.

E-commerce / gateway settlement fit: Rating: LOW as the primary/sole liquidity host; MEDIUM as an ancillary collections or multi-currency wallet layer. Pursuant to Spanish Law 21/2011 on electronic money and the PSD2-derived regime (Royal Decree-Law 19/2017, Royal Decree 130/2019), only an electronic-money institution (EMI) or payment institution authorised or passported in the EEA may lawfully provide e-money, payment accounts, and payment services in Spain. An offshore digital EMI (post-Brexit UK EMI, US or LatAm fintech) that lacks EEA passporting rights has no regulated access to the Spanish market: it cannot open Spanish IBAN accounts, settle Spanish staff costs, or receive Spanish debtor collections with the same legal comfort as a credit institution. Such offshore EMIs may be used purely as a technical add-in via a contractual agency model with an EEA-authorised EMI/bank; they cannot confer the creditor-protection, factoring-escrow, or LC-issuance capabilities needed for a licensed trade-finance company.

Stage 06

Corporate Tax & Transfer Pricing

Corporate income tax (CIT), box-by-box return breakdown, dividend WHT, and director personal liability.

Statutory corporate income tax (CIT)

25% general rate for Spanish resident companies. Newly incorporated entities may apply 15% during the first profitable tax period and the immediately following period, subject to statutory eligibility and anti-abuse rules.

Dividend withholding tax (WHT)

19% Spanish withholding tax on dividends paid by a Spanish resident company, subject to domestic exemptions and treaty reductions. Dividends to a qualifying EU parent may be exempt under the Parent-Subsidiary regime where the parent holds at least 10% of the Spanish subsidiary, satisfies the minimum holding-period and subject-to-tax requirements, and the anti-abuse conditions are met.

Mandatory Return Breakdown

Deadline: · Frequency:

Within 25 calendar days following the six-month period after the end of the tax year. For a calendar-year taxpayer, the standard deadline is 25 July.

Deadline: · Frequency:

Generally 1 to 20 April, October and December. The deadline moves to the next business day where applicable. Mandatory filing generally applies where the preceding tax period's net turnover exceeded EUR 6 million, with additional rules for consolidated groups.

Deadline: · Frequency:

Generally during the month following the ten-month period after the end of the tax period. For a calendar-year taxpayer, the ordinary filing window is November.

Deadline: · Frequency:

Generally filed during the first month of the calendar year following the year of payment, with the exact deadline determined by the AEAT filing calendar.

Transfer Pricing & Economic Substance

Master / Local File threshold: Local File documentation is generally required for related-party transactions exceeding EUR 250,000 in aggregate with the same related person or entity and within the same transaction type during the tax period, subject to statutory exclusions. Master File documentation is generally required for Spanish entities belonging to groups with consolidated annual revenue of at least EUR 45 million. Documentation exemptions and simplified documentation for smaller taxpayers do not remove the arm's-length requirement.

Economic substance scope: Spain does not operate a separate regime formally titled Economic Substance Regulations equivalent to certain offshore jurisdictions. Substance is nevertheless relevant under Spanish anti-abuse rules, beneficial-ownership requirements, the principal-purpose test, controlled foreign company rules, interest limitation rules, treaty interpretation and the general prohibition on simulation or tax-law abuse. A factoring SL should maintain Spanish decision-making, appropriate directors and personnel, risk control, systems, premises or operational capability, documented credit underwriting, servicing capacity, bank-account control, records and commercially supportable capital and financing arrangements. A conduit company with no genuine functions, assets, people or risk assumption may lose treaty benefits and face reassessment.

Fatal Compliance Red Lines & Director Liability

Corporate income tax evasion and fraudulent return

Statutory sanction: Tax fraud exceeding EUR 120,000 may constitute a criminal offense, generally punishable by imprisonment of one to five years and a fine of one to six times the defrauded amount. Aggravated cases, including amounts exceeding EUR 600,000 or use of interposed entities, may attract imprisonment of two to six years and a fine of two to six times the defrauded amount.

Director personal liability: Directors may incur criminal liability where they knowingly participate, civil liability for restitution and tax debt, and administrative disqualification consequences. Travel restrictions or precautionary asset measures may be ordered in serious proceedings; imprisonment is not automatic and requires judicial determination.
Unlicensed financial activity

Statutory sanction: Regulatory sanctions may include cessation orders, public censure, fines and other measures under the applicable financial-sector legislation. Where the business constitutes an establecimiento financiero de crédito, authorization, capital, governance, prudential, reporting and supervisory requirements apply.

Director personal liability: Directors and de facto managers may face administrative sanctions, civil liability for losses and, where conduct is fraudulent or unauthorized to a criminal degree, criminal prosecution. Personal sanctions depend on the specific regulatory statute and the director's involvement.
Transfer-pricing manipulation

Statutory sanction: The AEAT may adjust the Spanish tax base, impose tax penalties generally calculated by reference to the unpaid tax or incorrect data, and apply interest. Failure to provide required documentation can trigger specific documentation penalties, commonly calculated per missing or incorrect item and subject to statutory limits.

Director personal liability: Directors may face civil or tax liability where they deliberately approve abusive arrangements, falsify records or obstruct inspection. Ordinary TP errors generally create corporate rather than automatic personal liability.
Withholding tax failure

Statutory sanction: The Spanish payer remains liable for unpaid withholding, late-payment interest and applicable tax penalties. Penalties may generally range from 50% to 150% of the unpaid amount depending on severity, concealment and fraudulent conduct.

Director personal liability: Directors may incur subsidiary liability where statutory requirements for administrator liability are satisfied, particularly after failed collection from the company or where deliberate non-compliance is established.
AML, terrorist financing and suspicious transaction reporting

Statutory sanction: Under Spanish AML legislation, serious and very serious violations may attract substantial corporate fines, potentially reaching millions of euros or statutory percentages of net worth, own funds or annual turnover, together with public disclosure, authorization consequences and management disqualification.

Director personal liability: Members of the management body and compliance officers may be personally sanctioned where they consented to, enabled or negligently failed to prevent the breach. Criminal liability may arise for money laundering or terrorist financing, including imprisonment and asset confiscation.
Money laundering and proceeds-of-crime integration

Statutory sanction: Money laundering may result in imprisonment, fines, confiscation of proceeds and instruments, and disqualification. Corporate criminal liability may apply where the offense is committed for the company's benefit due to deficient supervision or control.

Director personal liability: Directors, beneficial owners and de facto managers may face imprisonment, fines, confiscation, civil restitution and precautionary travel or asset restrictions ordered by a court.
Shell company, beneficial-owner concealment and tax residence abuse

Statutory sanction: Consequences may include denial of treaty benefits, recharacterization of transactions, corporate tax and withholding reassessments, interest, tax penalties and potential criminal tax or fraud proceedings.

Director personal liability: Directors and beneficial owners may face veil-piercing arguments, civil restitution, tax liability, disqualification and criminal liability where they intentionally concealed ownership or participated in fraudulent arrangements.
False accounting and fraudulent receivables

Statutory sanction: Potential consequences include accounting and corporate fraud prosecution, contractual rescission, creditor claims, damages, confiscation and tax reassessment. Criminal penalties depend on the offense and loss amount.

Director personal liability: Directors may incur personal criminal and civil liability, including restitution to creditors, disqualification from management, asset preservation measures and imprisonment where statutory elements are proven.
Interest limitation and unlawful financing deductions

Statutory sanction: Disallowed deductions, tax-base increases, withholding reassessments, late-payment interest and tax penalties may apply. Anti-abuse, debt-equity and transfer-pricing rules may recharacterize the arrangement.

Director personal liability: Personal liability is not automatic but may arise for intentional tax fraud, fraudulent insolvency, asset stripping or knowing approval of sham financing.
Sanctions, export-control and restricted-party breach

Statutory sanction: Administrative fines, transaction blocking, license restrictions, asset freezes and criminal penalties may apply under EU and Spanish sanctions legislation. The exact consequence depends on the applicable sanctions regime and conduct.

Director personal liability: Directors and compliance personnel may face personal administrative or criminal exposure for knowing participation, willful blindness or grossly deficient controls. Asset and travel restrictions may be imposed by competent authorities or courts.
